input.text: Welcome to 798 — where a cold-war electronics factory became China's contemporary art capital. These vast halls were built in the nineteen fifties with East German assistance, in genuine Bauhaus style: look up at the sawtooth roofs, angled north so uniform, soft light would pour into the workshops — a factory designed like a photographer's studio. The plant made military electronics for decades, then fell silent. In the early two-thousands, starving artists discovered what collectors now pay fortunes for: those chimneys, pipes, and red propaganda slogans painted on factory walls became the raw aesthetic of Chinese contemporary art. Galleries moved in, then museums, then the world — today 798 hosts hundreds of galleries and design shops, and its exhibitions range from ink painting to digital art. No ticket needed to wander. Grab a coffee in a former workshop, and let the factory walls surprise you — this is where today's China argues with its own history, in paint and steel.
